title: What is known about 1RB---_1RC1LE_0RD0RF_0RE0LA_1LF0LB_1LA1LD
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB---_1RC1LE_0RD0RF_0RE0LA_1LF0LB_1LA1LD.
intro: Nobody knows whether this machine halts from blank tape, and it may be hard to ever know: its run is a Collatz-like iteration. Each time the head, in state C, stands at the right end of the tape, the tape is 1^4 0 (10)^x 1^m with the head on a cell s; a six-case map sends (x, m, s) to the next such moment, and one case of the map is the halt. Lean proves that this map describes the machine exactly: the machine halts from blank tape if and only if the orbit of (7, 1, 0) under the map reaches the halting case. This page explains the map and why the halting question becomes a question about powers of two.
verdict: The question is open, and Collatz-like. The run follows a map on (x, m, s), and Lean proves it: the machine halts from blank tape if and only if the map's orbit from (7, 1, 0) reaches the halting case. That happens exactly when, during a chain of doubling steps, x lands on one particular value; iterating the map shows no such landing in the first 10,000 rounds, which is far beyond 10100 machine steps, but nothing rules it out in general.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (A1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 23,223 cells have been visited and 20,762 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: No halt in the first 4.84·10<sup>772</sup> steps (accelerated run, blocks of 2)
claims.text: The run-length simulator tools/py/bbtools/rleaccel_rec.py (blocks of 2 cells, runs crossed in one step, cycle jumps used only after a symbolic proof of the one-cycle rule, and proofs that may themselves apply earlier rules to symbolic lengths, with exact polynomial step counts; tested cell for cell against direct runs) runs 60,620,000 macro steps from blank tape without a halt, in 300 seconds. That is more than 4.84·10772 machine steps. It found no rule that repeats forever, so it does not decide the machine.

claims.title: Growth shape: power/power
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.163). Right of the start it grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.654).

claims.title: Rules B and R of the map
claims.text: For all n, x: from K(x+1, 2n, s) the machine reaches K(x, 2n+4, 1−s) (rule B, 6n+12 or 6n+10 steps), and from K(0, 2n, s) it reaches K(n+3, 1, 0) for s = 0 and K(n+3, 3, 0) for s = 1 (rule R). Here K(x, m, s) is 1^4 0 (10)^x 1^m with the head in C on s at the right end, blank beyond.

claims.title: Rules A, A' and C of the map, for all parameters
claims.text: For all parameters: rule C, K(i+n+3, 2n+1, 0) reaches K(i, 4n+9, 0) and K(i+n+3, 2n+1, 1) reaches K(i, 4n+8, 1); rule A, K(j+2, 2(j+1+k)+1, s) reaches K(2j+5, 2k+3, 1−s), and K(j+2, 2j+1, 1) reaches K(2j+5, 1, 0); rule A′, K(j+2, 2j+1, 0) reaches K(2j+7, 1, 0); and A for x = 1. Rules A and C share their first two parts: a start piece, then one inner cycle per 10 pair moved (chained by an induction written by hand); each ends with its own end piece. Every piece is proved by bbtools.symtm.

claims.title: Halting is equivalent to the orbit reaching H
claims.text: step_ok: from every sample K(x, m, s) the machine reaches the sample the map gives, in at least one step, or (case H) halts. start: from blank tape it reaches K(7, 1, 0) after 216 steps. halts_iff: the machine halts from blank tape if and only if the orbit of (7, 1, 0) under the map (mstep, orbit) reaches the case H. nonhalt_of_orbit: if the orbit never reaches H, the machine never halts. Axioms: propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only.

claims.title: The halting case
claims.text: From K(0, 2n+1, s), for every n, the machine runs into its halting transition (A reads a 1) after 2n+11 (s = 0) or 2n+9 (s = 1) steps.

claims.title: The whole map holds for the first 10<sup>10</sup> steps
claims.text: Every sample from step 216 on (the head in C at the right end) has the form K(x, m, s), except one sample inside each R step where the tape is solid, and each sample follows from the previous one by the map: py/samplemap.py check, using tools/c/tmrun.c. See the README for the counts.

claims.title: The map agrees with the machine on all small samples
claims.text: Started from K(x, m, s) for every x < 25, m < 30 and every x < 45, odd m < 70 (both s), the machine reaches the sample the map predicts (or halts where the map says H). This found the boundary case A′, which the run itself meets only once, before step 216.

claims.title: The halting condition is a near-power-of-2 condition
claims.text: Only rule C with s = 0 can lead to the halting case. Along a chain of such C steps m runs through (m+7)2<sup>i</sup> − 7, and Lean proves, by induction on the chain length, that a chain from (x, m, 0) ends in H exactly when x + k + 1 = (m+7)(2<sup>k+1</sup>−1)/2 for some k ≥ 0 (after an R step with m = 1: x = 2<sup>k+3</sup> − k − 5), and otherwise leaves through A or A′. So the machine halts from blank tape iff some point of the orbit meets this condition.

claims.title: No halt in the first 200 rounds, checked exactly
claims.text: Lean follows the orbit of (7, 1, 0) exactly, with each whole B phase as one jump (proved equal to x steps of rule B by induction on x). Lean's kernel evaluates 12,815 jumps: 91,065,045,402,056,075,917,728,632,641,862,099 (about 9.1·10<sup>34</sup>) steps of the map, 200 R steps, no H. The first 20 rounds, which carry almost all of the heuristic chance of a hit, are a separate theorem (271 jumps, 109,233 map steps). Since each map step is at least one machine step, the machine runs more than 9.1·10<sup>34</sup> steps from blank tape without halting.

claims.title: No halt of the map in 10,000 rounds
claims.text: Iterating the map from K(7, 1, 0) (the sample at step 216), with whole B phases applied at once, gives 10,000 R steps, 29,225,208 C steps and 25,330 A steps without reaching the halting case; x then has thousands of bits, so this is far beyond any number of machine steps one could simulate. Since the map is a theorem, this shows that the machine does not halt in its first 10,000 rounds (the iteration itself is a Python computation).

claims.title: Why a halt looks very unlikely
claims.text: If the remainder at the end of each doubling chain were spread evenly, a chain whose last step has h = (m+5)/2 would halt with chance about 1/h. Summed over the orbit this gives 0.3187 in all, but almost all of it in the first 20 rounds (which, and the first 200 rounds, Lean's kernel checks exactly: no hit); rounds 21 to 1,000 add less than 10<sup>−4</sup>, and rounds after 200 less than 10<sup>−30</sup> (every chain there ends at h > 2<sup>115</sup>), and x gains about 0.58 bits per round (583 bits at round 1,000), so the rest is negligible. The remainders look spread over all of [0, h), somewhat more often near 0 (in 1,000 rounds the 1,409 chain ends fall 192 into the lowest tenth and 88 into the highest), so nothing rules a hit out either: this is evidence, not proof.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. Lean reduces the question exactly to the map: the machine halts iff the orbit of (7, 1, 0) reaches H. What is missing is a proof that the orbit never meets the halting condition (x + k + 1 = (m+7)(2<sup>k+1</sup>−1)/2 at the start of a doubling chain), a Collatz-type problem; the first 200 rounds are checked exactly and meet no hit; heuristically a halt is very unlikely but nothing excludes it.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same table as 1RB1RF_1LC---_1LE1RD_1RA0RC_0LF0LA_0LD0RB up to renaming and mirroring, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows, and the answer may be as hard as a Collatz question. The run is a simple map on two numbers, and it stops exactly when one of them lands on a value just below a power of two.

facts.text: No halt in the run-length accelerator (proved cycle jumps, blocks of 2).
the orbit followed exactly in Lean's kernel, no hit: more than 9.1·10<sup>34</sup> machine steps without a halt
all six cases of the map proved in Lean for all parameters, chained from blank tape
the map, iterated, does not reach its halting case, so the machine does not halt in that many rounds
No halt in the C simulator; 23,223 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.

sections.heading: Two counters and a six-case map
html: Watch the machine each time the head, in state C, is at the right end of the tape. From step 216 on, the tape then always reads 1^4 0 (10)^x 1^m: four 1s, a 0, x copies of 10, and a block of m 1s, with the head on one more cell s (0 or 1) just right of the block. At step 216 it is (x, m, s) = (7, 1, 0).

From one such moment to the next, (x, m, s) changes by one of these rules:

  • B (m even, x ≥ 1): (x−1, m+4, 1−s). One 10 pair is turned into four more 1s.
  • R (m even, x = 0): ((m+6)/2, 1 or 3, 0). The block is turned back into pairs; the new m is 1 if s was 0 and 3 if s was 1.
  • A (m odd, x < (m+5)/2): (2x+1, m−2x+4, 1−s). The pairs double. (One boundary case differs: x = (m+3)/2 with s = 0 gives (2x+3, 1, 0).)
  • C (m odd, x ≥ (m+5)/2): (x−(m+5)/2, 2m+7−s, s). The block doubles, paid for with pairs.
  • H (m odd, x = 0): the machine halts.

So a round looks like this: after R the block is tiny and x is large; a chain of C steps doubles the block, using up pairs, until an A step doubles the pairs again; then the block is even and the B steps pour all pairs into it, one at a time, until x = 0 and R starts the next round. Each round roughly doubles the size of everything, and the time per round roughly quadruples.

sections.heading: Exact tapes, exact step counts
html:
The same map written the way the bbchallenge wiki writes Antihydra's: name the tape exactly, then list the rules, each with the exact number of machine steps it takes. One family, the samples of lean/MapThm.lean (Kc), with the head in state C reading s:

K(x, m, s) := 0∞ 14 0 (10)x 1m C>s 0∞ (s = 0 or 1)

rulefrom → tostepswhen
start0∞ A> 0∞ → K(7, 1, 0)216
BK(x + 1, m, s) → K(x, m + 4, 1 − s)3m + 12 − 2sm even
RK(0, m, s) → K((m + 6)/2, 1 + 2s, 0)6m + 55 + 4sm even
CK(x, m, s) → K(x − (m + 5)/2, 2m + 7 − s, s)(3m2 + 24m + 61)/2 − 7sm odd, x ≥ (m + 5)/2
AK(x, m, s) → K(2x + 1, m + 4 − 2x, 1 − s)6x2 + 12x + 3m + 43 − 2sm odd, 1 ≤ x ≤ (m + 3)/2, not A′
A′K(x, 2x − 3, 0) → K(2x + 3, 1, 0)6x2 + 30x + 75x ≥ 2
halt (H)K(0, m, s) → haltm + 11 − 2sm odd; A reads 1

The rows are the six cases of mstep, and every one is a theorem in Lean (step_ok, with halts_iff: the machine halts from blank tape iff the orbit of (7, 1, 0) reaches the halt row). Which step counts are in Lean: the start (start, exactly 216 steps), B and R (ruleB0, ruleB1, ruleR0, ruleR1 in lean/Rules.lean, with these counts) and the halt (toHalt0, toHalt1: m + 10 − 2s steps to the cell where A reads a 1, then the halting transition). Rules A, A′ and C are proved in Lean as "reaches in at least one step" (ruleA0, ruleA1, ruleA1z, ruleAp, ruleC0, ruleC1); the pieces they are chained from carry step counts (ph1_0, cyc_0, fin_0, endA0, … in lean/Rules.lean), but their totals in the table are checked against direct simulation only, not stated in Lean. py/exact.py checks every row on 3,772 samples (x ≤ 40, m ≤ 45, both s; 46 of them halting) and on the 1,140 samples the rows predict in the first 107 steps from blank tape, each equal to the machine's tape at its predicted step.

For example K(10, 1, 0), a tape that halts: rule C (44 steps) gives K(7, 9, 0), rule C again (260 steps) gives K(0, 25, 0), and the halt row adds 36: 340 steps in all, which is what direct simulation gives.

sections.heading: Landing just below a power of two
html: The halt needs m odd and x = 0. Rules A, A′, B and R never produce that, and rule C with s = 1 makes m even. So the only way in is a C step with s = 0 that uses up the pairs exactly: x = (m+5)/2. In a chain of C steps with s = 0 the block runs through m, 2m+7, 4m+21, … = (m+7)2i − 7, so the chain halts exactly when the starting x equals (m+7)(2k+1−1)/2 − k − 1 for some k.

For the chains right after an R step with m = 1, that is x = 2k+3 − k − 5: 3, 10, 25, 56, 119, 246, … So the machine stops if and only if, at the start of some chain, the number of pairs is one of these values just below a power of two. Nothing in the map seems to prevent that; it just has not happened. This is the same kind of question as the Collatz problem: easy to state, easy to test, and with no known way to settle it.

A rough count of the chances (about 1/h for a chain ending at size h) adds up to about 0.32, nearly all of it in the first 20 rounds; later rounds are so large that their chances are tiny. Lean's kernel follows the orbit exactly through the first 200 rounds, which carry all of that count except less than 10−30, and finds no hit. The table lists every doubling chain of the first 20 rounds: where it starts, how many C steps it makes, and the remainder y it ends with, out of the h = (M+5)/2 pairs the next step would need. The machine halts iff some chain ends with y = 0. The closest call is in round 10, a remainder of 16 out of 1,279.
So a halt looks very unlikely, but nothing in the map rules it out: beyond the checked rounds the remainders still look spread over all of [0, h).

sections.heading: The map is a theorem
html: Lean proves every case of the map for all values of x, m and s. Rules B and R are single sweeps. Rules A and C start the same way: the head walks into the block, and then one inner cycle per 10 pair moves a pair from the left into the block of 1s, (10)^i (11)^j E>111 0 (10)^k becoming (10)^(i-1) (11)^(j+2) E>111 0 (10)^(k-1). Lean chains any number of cycles by induction. C ends when the right-hand pairs run out first, A when the left-hand ones do; each ending is a separate symbolic run.

From blank tape the machine reaches K(7, 1, 0) after 216 steps, a finite computation that Lean's kernel checks. Put together, the theorem halts_iff says: the machine halts from blank tape if and only if the orbit of (7, 1, 0) under the map reaches H. All of the Turing machine is gone from the question; only the arithmetic remains.

Two more steps are proved on top of the map. lean/Chain.lean proves the halting condition by induction on the length of a doubling chain: a chain ends in H exactly when its starting x is (m+7)(2k+1−1)/2 − k − 1, and otherwise it leaves through rule A or A′. lean/Early.lean runs the orbit inside Lean, with a whole B phase as one jump (proved by induction), and the kernel checks 200 rounds without H, about 9.1·1034 steps of the map.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.163). Right of the start it grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.654).
After 109 steps the tape spans 23,223 cells (210 left of the start, 20,472 right), with a density of 1s of 0.894.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

family: Collatz-like map on two counters (halts iff an orbit hits a near-power of 2)
summary: A six-case map on two counters, (10)^x and 1^m, proved in Lean to describe the run exactly; the machine halts iff a doubling chain of the map lands on x = (m+7)(2^(k+1)-1)/2 - k - 1, a Collatz-like condition (proved in Lean); the first 200 rounds are checked exactly in Lean's kernel, with no hit. Accelerated run: no halt in 4.84e772 steps.
